papers.title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
papers.abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

papers.title: Systematic Spike Sorting Errors Revealed by Juxtacellular Ground Truth in the Awake Brain
papers.abstract: Existing ground-truth data for spike sorting come almost entirely from anesthetized or in vitro preparations. Yet phenomena expected to challenge spike sorting most (spike overlap and bursting) depend on brain state and differ in the awake brain. Therefore, error estimates from existing benchmarks may not transfer to awake recordings, and the types of errors in the awake brain remain largely uncharacterized. To address this, we generated a ground-truth dataset (16 neurons) using paired juxtacellular-extracellular electrophysiology in awake mice, and found spike sorting performance, particularly recall, to be lower than conventional benchmarks might suggest. Generally, false negatives sharply increased with intrinsic physiological factors like bursting, whereas false positives were more strongly associated with extrinsic factors, such as putative spike overlaps. To quantify contributions to errors from intrinsic and extrinsic factors, for each observed juxtacellular waveform we predicted the corresponding extracellular waveform. In the best-performing sorter, we estimate approximately half of false positives were attributable to credulous attempts to resolve putative overlaps. Bursting and putative overlaps were each associated with a roughly doubled false negative rate when they occurred separately, and with a sevenfold increase when they occurred together. These co-occurrences accounted for approximately 40% of a typical neuron's false negatives, despite comprising only approximately a fifth of its spikes. Thus, the moments when spike sorters must rely on the assumption of waveform invariance the most to resolve overlaps are exactly the moments when bursting makes that assumption least valid. We also estimate that three-quarters of false negatives had been detected but assigned to other units. These spikes were not cleanly oversplit: post-hoc merging was not productive because the loss in precision was three times the gain in recall. Because bursting and spike overlaps often co-occur, sorting spikes by waveform similarity and repairing the result by post hoc merging is unlikely to adequately balance precision and recall in the situations of greatest scientific interest. That is, while bursting and spike overlaps may involve only a minority of spikes, the resulting sorting errors may disproportionately distort the interpretation of neuronal population dynamics. We thus conclude that uncertainty quantification in sorters' output is essential.

papers.title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
papers.abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
papers.abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

papers.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
papers.abstract: Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

papers.title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
papers.abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.

papers.title: Standard touchscreen test procedures shift circadian rhythms in mice: a modified protocol to minimize circadian confounds
papers.abstract: Touchscreen based cognitive testing for rodents offers considerable experimental benefits, including a semi automated battery approach and the use of appetitive rather than aversive reinforcement. However, food reward and touchscreen illumination introduce potential confounds, as both food and light can shift, entrain, or disrupt circadian rhythms, which in turn can affect learning and memory. The potential for the test apparatus to impact endogenous circadian rhythms is particularly problematic when probing relationships between sleep, circadian disruption, and cognitive performance. After observing phase shifting of circadian rhythms in nocturnal mice tested using standard touchscreen test procedures, which include testing during the active period (early lights off), we evaluated the relative contributions of the illuminated screen and the appetitive food reward. Our results indicate that light emitted by the touchscreen chambers is responsible for the circadian phase shifting effects, with standard screen conditions inducing a ~3.5 h phase delay in daily activity rhythms when training is conducted early in the dark period for 7 consecutive days. We then modified lighting in the test environment and the home cage to identify parameters that would minimize circadian shifting without impairing visual discrimination or performance on a widely used cognitive test (Trial Unique Nonmatching to Location, TUNL). From the 10 conditions tested, we offer specific recommendations for modifying touchscreen test protocols to minimize circadian confounds, without impacting task acquisition or performance.

papers.title: Circadian feeding rhythm loss drives sex-specific β-cell dysfunction in diet-induced obesity
papers.abstract: Diet-induced obesity (DIO), modeled by a high-fat diet (HFD), adversely affects circadian glucose homeostasis partly by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles. However, its impact on circadian {beta}-cell function and relevant transcriptional programs remains unclear. To investigate this, we exposed male and female C57BL/6 mice to either chow or HFD for eight weeks and assessed behavioral (feeding/activity), physiological (glucose tolerance/insulin secretion), transcriptomic (RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)), and epigenomic (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using Sequencing (ATAC-seq)) circadian rhythms. Additionally, we tested whether normalizing fasting/feeding cycles via time-restricted feeding (tRF) during the dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle could mitigate DIO's deleterious effects. DIO disrupted circadian fasting/feeding rhythms, with greater disruption in males than females (p<0.05 vs. CHOW). In males, DIO abolished circadian regulation of glucose tolerance and in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (p<0.05 vs. chow), whereas female mice maintained circadian glucose homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis of male islets revealed a 42.1% reduction in circadian-regulated transcripts under DIO, with weakened rhythms in key {beta}-cell pathways such as insulin secretion. Moreover, ATAC-Seq analysis indicated reduced chromatin accessibility of genes/pathways related to insulin secretion and glucose hemostasis under DIO (p<0.05 vs. chow) during both dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle. Notably, dark-phase time-restricted feeding (tRF) restored circadian glucose tolerance, GSIS, and islet gene expression, whereas light-phase tRF enhanced {beta}-cell function during the normally inactive/light phase of the circadian cycle, further suppressing circadian rhythmicity of the islet transcriptome. Motif analysis indicated that DIO suppressed the activity of D-box transcription factors (TFs) (DBP and TEF) while enhancing the activity of ETS family TFs (ELK1, ETS2, ELF2, and GABPA), which was partly mitigated by dark-phase tRF. Our study demonstrates that DIO disrupts circadian {beta}-cell function and gene expression by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles in male mice and reveals significant sex differences in how DIO affects circadian glucose homeostasis and {beta}-cell function.

papers.title: Circadian multimodal physiological, ocular and behavioural data from a 40-hour forced-desynchrony protocol
papers.abstract: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.

papers.title: Intrinsic fluctuations modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of human conscious perception
papers.abstract: Human conscious perception is not determined solely by external sensory input but is also shaped by moment-to-moment fluctuations in intrinsic brain states. However, how these intrinsic states directly function after stimulus onset to shape the emergence of conscious perception remains unclear. We recorded sEEG activity in thalamus and five other consciousness-related cortical regions, while 32 patients (n= 2,023 recording sites) conscious percept a near-threshold visual stimulus. Preceding the extensively evoked consciousness-related activities, there are early activities (0-200ms after stimulus onset) exclusively appeared in high-order thalamus. These early activities inversely associated with stimulus strength, which reflected an intrinsic state that compensated for the stimulus-evoked response to reach the conscious threshold. These early activities were closer to the critical state in conscious trials, which enables more efficient information processing. These results suggest that intrinsic fluctuations in the high-order thalamus directly modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of conscious perception.

papers.title: NTAD: A longitudinal neuroimaging dataset of Alzheimer's disease pathology
papers.abstract: We introduce the New Therapeutics in Alzheimer's Disease (NTAD) dataset, a multi-modal and longitudinal imaging dataset from 70 biomarker-positive people with early dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer's Disease (AD), assessed over 2.5 years, and 35 healthy controls assessed at baseline. The data include simultaneous magneto- and electro-encephalography (M/EEG), 3-Tesla structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), Amyloid-beta; positron emission tomography (PET), fluid proteomic biomarkers in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, and a battery of clinical and neuropsychological assessments. 11C UCB-J PET was undertaken for a subset of participants. For people with AD, assessments were repeated at approximately three weeks, 15 months, and 28 months after baseline. The data can be accessed through the Dementias Platform UK (DPUK), including pre-processed M/EEG and T1 MRI in pseudonymised BIDS format. With the pressing need to develop treatments for slowing, reversing, and preventing AD, these data provide an opportunity for identifying and validating novel biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease neurophysiology, as well as understanding its treatable pathology.

papers.title: Hierarchical Uncertainty Transformation During Multimodal Comprehension
papers.abstract: Human communication requires combining information from different modalities even when each source is incomplete or ambiguous. Yet how uncertainty is coordinated as distinct semantic representations interact and converge remains unclear. Here we propose a hierarchical uncertainty transformation framework and test it across four gesture-speech experiments combining behavioral measures, information-theoretic modelling, and electroencephalography. Rather than being uniformly reduced as information accumulates, uncertainty changed its computational form across three interdependent levels: uncertainty within modality-specific semantic representations, bidirectional but asymmetric changes during cross-modal interaction, and uncertainty associated with multisensory convergence. These computational distinctions were accompanied by differentiated but temporally overlapping neural associations. Modality-specific uncertainty was expressed relatively early, whereas cross-modal transformation and convergence were most prominently associated with activity in the N400 range. Critically, both the neural expression and statistical coupling of these computational quantities varied with the semantic information available from gesture and speech. Together, these findings show that multimodal comprehension involves a context-dependent reorganization of uncertainty across interacting representations, providing a computational framework for understanding how coherent meaning emerges from heterogeneous and uncertain information.

papers.title: Cortical bursts provide spatio-temporal frames for the large-scale phase synchrony emerging across the birth transition
papers.abstract: Structural corticocortical connectivity grows rapidly around birth, but how it establishes the large-scale neuronal interactions needed for lifelong neurocognitive performance remains unclear. Using repeated high-density EEG from 233 preterm-born infants recorded at 33-45 weeks postmenstrual age, we characterized the development of three phase-based interaction modes with distinct temporal relationships to cortical bursts: burst-based, burst-framed, and general phase-based connectivity. Burst-framed connectivity was quantified with a novel metric, nested phase-phase correlation. All three modes declined globally with age but differed spatially: burst-based connectivity became more confined, burst-framed connectivity reorganized towards sensorimotor-association connectivity, whereas general phase-based connectivity retained a stable modular organization. General phase-based connectivity was initially concentrated along burst-framed connections, but this coupling weakened with age. Its greater persistence around term age was associated with poorer neurocognitive outcomes, suggesting delayed network maturation. These findings suggest that bursting may transiently scaffold the maturation of large-scale corticocortical phase synchrony across the birth transition.

papers.title: Partial agonists and heteromeric Kainate receptor desensitization
papers.abstract: Kainate receptors (KARs) are glutamate-gated ion channels that mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. KARs assemble as homo- or heterotetramers composed of five subunits (GluK1-5), with heteromeric assemblies representing the predominant native population. Although KARs share overall structures and basic functional properties with other ionotropic glutamate receptor subfamilies, they exhibit distinct gating kinetics, particularly with respect to desensitization. While earlier studies have demonstrated how agonist binding drives gate opening and subsequent desensitization, the mechanisms governing partial agonism and desensitization of KARs, especially in heteromeric KARs, remain incompletely understood. Here, we combine electrophysiology and microscale thermophoresis binding assays to elucidate how distinct KAR partial agonists control KAR desensitization and its recovery. While the onset rates of desensitization of homo- and heteromeric receptors activated by high/saturating concentrations of partial agonists are conserved between GluK2 and GluK2/GluK5 receptors, recovery from desensitization in heteromers is significantly slower than in homomers. Together with structural modeling and analysis of the GluK2 and GluK5 ligand binding domains (LBDs) in complex with orthosteric ligands, we show that agonist residence time and the extent of LBD bi-lobe closure across various agonists take precedence over subunit composition in governing KAR desensitization.

papers.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

papers.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
papers.abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

papers.title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
papers.abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.

papers.title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
papers.abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

papers.title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

papers.title: Reducing the Risk of Gradient Induced EEG Hardware Heating During Simultaneous EEG-fMRI
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) has the potential to provide a more complete characterisation of brain function. Acquiring these data simultaneously requires the EEG hardware to be MR safe, since the EEG cap, amplifiers and powerpacks must be located within the MR environment. Placing them in this environment exposes them to both static and varying (radiofrequency (RF) and gradient) magnetic fields, presenting a potential heating risk. Previous studies have typically positioned the amplifiers and powerpacks outside of the bore, meaning that this risk is largely limited to the EEG cap. However, current guidelines recommend positioning the amplifiers within the bore. This reduces the distance between the EEG electrodes and amplifier, improving EEG signal quality and reducing risks of RF heating at the electrodes, but presents a potential heating risk for the amplifiers and powerpacks from the varying magnetic field gradients. In this study, we demonstrate that placing the amplifiers and powerpacks in the bore presents a significant heating risk, both at 7T and 3T. At 7T, we show that EPI sequences with a slew rate of at least 88 T/m/s resulted in significant heating of the EEG amplifiers. This heating effect could be negated by reducing the slew rate to 61 T/m/s. At 3T, we replicate the EEG amplifier heating and show that an alternative approach to reducing the gradient slew rates experience by the hardware is to increase the distance between the EEG amplifier/powerpacks and the isocentre of the magnet. Increasing the distance between the EEG hardware and MR isocentre by 30 cm mitigates the heating risk to the amplifiers and powerpacks, regardless of sequence parameters (e.g., slew rate). Therefore, whilst reducing the distance between the electrodes and amplifiers may improve EEG signal quality and reduce the potential for electrode RF heating, we show that risk of heating of hardware by gradient switching is greatly increased. This is particularly important to consider with the faster gradient slew rates available on modern MRI scanners, desired to increase spatial resolution. Experimenters must make careful decisions about hardware placement to ensure that the EEG-fMRI setup they use is safe, taking account of the varying risks that are posed by different approaches.

papers.title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice
papers.abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 10 microM and an EC of ~3.4 microM. This inhibition was mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABAA receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem.

papers.title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
papers.abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

papers.title: RyR2-Mediated Ca2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Background Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent-verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: Disambiguation of two-tone images aligns object representations in the EEG
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological responses to visual objects carry information about stimulus identity and semantic category, but it remains difficult to know whether such information represents conceptual knowledge or merely regularities in physical image features. Here, we presented two-tone images before and after disambiguation via corresponding photographs to seventeen healthy participants while recording EEG to dissociate the learned image concept from its physical properties. After disambiguation, EEG responses to learned two-tone images became more similar to the responses of their photo counterparts. This effect emerged approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset and peaked at 350 ms. However, we found no evidence for a generalization of the response pattern to the stimulus semantic category. Furthermore, alignment to the photo counterparts was only detectable after explicit visual disambiguation rather than spontaneous recognition. Together, these findings indicate that EEG can capture specific learned conceptual modulations of responses to visually degraded stimuli, while also showing that low-level visual properties dominate the representational structure.

papers.title: Turning an object into a scene: buildings activate scene-selective visual cortex independently of visual features
papers.abstract: Human visual cortex contains regions that selectively respond to both scenes and large objects, particularly buildings. The cortical overlap between buildings and scenes has been attributed to shared visual features (e.g., cardinal orientations, rectilinearity). Alternative accounts propose that buildings may also activate scene representations indirectly, independently of specific visual features, for example because buildings evoke a sense of space. Here, we tested for such feature-independent activation by comparing EEG and fMRI responses in human participants (both sexes) to buildings and visually-matched boxes, and relating these responses to scene-selective responses. Buildings and boxes were matched using image-based metrics, deep neural networks, and a perceptual similarity task. Time-resolved EEG decoding showed that buildings and boxes evoked discriminable responses from 360ms post-stimulus onset, incompatible with feedforward visual feature processing. Importantly, the building-box classifier generalized to discriminate scenes from chairs, providing the first EEG evidence for a representational overlap between buildings and scenes. Temporal generalization analyses further showed that the late building-selective response corresponded to an earlier scene-selective response, with a temporal offset of ~130ms. Finally, ultra-fast fMRI (TR=140ms) revealed that the scene-selective parahippocampal place area (PPA) similarly showed a feature-independent building-selective response that was delayed and prolonged relative to the scene-selective response. These results clarify the nature of building selectivity in visual cortex by showing that this selectivity is feature-independent and delayed relative to scene selectivity. We propose that intrinsic associations between object categories (e.g., buildings and scenes, tools and hands) may account for part of the categorical organization of ventral temporal cortex.

papers.title: A Biologically Inspired Attention Model for Neural Signal Analysis
papers.abstract: Understanding how the brain represents sensory information and triggers behavioural responses is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Recent advances in neuronal recording techniques aim to progress towards this milestone, yet the resulting high-dimensional responses are challenging to interpret and link to relevant variables. Although existing machine learning models propose to do so, they often sacrifice interpretability for predictive power, effectively operating as black boxes. In this work, we introduce SPARKS, a biologically inspired model capable of high decoding accuracy and interpretable discovery within a single framework. SPARKS adapts the self-attention mechanism of large language models to extract information from the timing of single spikes and the sequence in which neurons fire using Hebbian learning. Trained with a criterion inspired by predictive coding to enforce temporal coherence, our model produces low-dimensional latent embeddings that are robust across sessions and animals. By directly capturing the underlying data distribution through a generative encoding-decoding framework, SPARKS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art decoders across diverse electrophysiology and calcium imaging datasets from the motor, visual and entorhinal cortices. Crucially, the Hebbian coefficients learned by the model are interpretable, allowing us to infer directed functional interactions and recover the known functional hierarchy of the mouse visual cortex. Overall, SPARKS unifies representation learning, high-performance decoding and model interpretability in a single framework by bridging neuroscience and AI, providing a powerful and versatile tool for dissecting neural computations and marking a step towards the next generation of biologically inspired intelligent systems.

papers.title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
papers.abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

papers.title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
papers.abstract: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere. Volumes were normalised to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) and related to age and SES (Hollingshead index) using Pearson correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; partial correlations adjusted for sex (age) and for age and sex (SES) served as sensitivity analyses. Results: Older age was associated with lower normalised volume of the right posterior subunit (r = -.456, q < .001) and the left posterior subunit (r = -.274, q = .007); both associations persisted after adjustment for sex. Lower SES showed a trend towards larger left anterior-inferior volume (r = .242, uncorrected p = .005) that did not survive FDR correction (q = .053). Conclusions: Age-related volumetric differences in the healthy hypothalamus appear to be concentrated in its posterior portion, a region housing arousal-promoting circuitry. Automated subunit segmentation offers a scalable tool for studying the hypothalamus in ageing and in relation to environmental exposures; the cross-sectional associations reported here should not be interpreted as causal or as within-person change.

papers.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
papers.abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

papers.title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
papers.abstract: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS. However, no specific regional driver of this signal was evident. Alternatively, components identified through sensorimotor template matching revealed a significant influence of -band power on MPS both at baseline and post-HFS. However, only a small number of these components genuinely localised to pre- or post-central gyri, and test-retest reliability of -band power was poor. Together, these findings indicate that resting-state EEG may be useful for tracking changes in cortical -band oscillations alongside the development of pain sensitivity. However, methods of sensorimotor component identification evidenced limited agreement and global PAF slowing could not be linked to a specific electrode grouping.

papers.title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
papers.abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS-EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.

papers.title: Clustering instantaneous phase-locking states with a rank-two Bures-Wasserstein distance
papers.abstract: Instantaneous phase-locking (iPL) matrices, defined by the cosines of pairwise phase differences between band-limited signals, underpin widely used methods for time-resolved functional connectivity, including Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA). Each iPL matrix has rank at most two and is fully characterized by its two nonzero eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. Yet, existing methods retain different parts of this decomposition and compare them using distances that do not reflect the geometry of the underlying sample space. We show that weighting the two eigenvectors by the square roots of their eigenvalues recovers each channel's phase relative to the mean phase, and that optimal orthogonal Procrustes alignment of these weighted eigenvector pairs yields the Bures-Wasserstein distance between the corresponding iPL matrices. In EEG, where most channels oscillate nearly in phase, existing distances become insensitive to phase-lag size, whereas the Bures-Wasserstein distance preserves this sensitivity. In simulations, clustering with this distance recovered states differing in both lag size and spatial pattern that existing distances failed to distinguish.In resting-state EEG, it resolved distinct phase-gradient states that other methods merged into a single global in-phase state.

papers.title: Chronic Sleep Disruption Activates the Transcriptional Unfolded Protein Response and Induces Compartment-Specific Proteomic Changes in Mice
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption (SD) is associated with adverse brain health and increased risk of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the pathological mechanisms underlying this association are not fully understood. Preclinical studies have shown that acute SD impairs cognition by altering vulnerable synapses (molecular composition, ultrastructure, and function). However, the cumulative effects of chronic SD on the adult brain and its vulnerable synapses, that might contribute to AD risk, remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of chronic SD on brain transcriptomic signatures and subcellular compartment-specific proteomic profiles to identify genes, proteins, and signaling pathways that might confer AD risk. Chronic SD induced a modest transcriptional stress response globally, whereas alterations were more pronounced in the synaptosomal (synapse-enriched P2 fractions) and whole-brain proteomes. Remarkably, chronic SD elicited unique proteomic alterations at the synaptic compartment were distinct from whole-brain effects, including increased proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, regulation of dendritic spine morphogenesis, and regulation of long-term synaptic depression, compared to increased proteins involved in immune/inflammatory, glial responses and neuronal function at the whole-brain level. Consistent with the chronic SD-induced molecular signatures, we observed subtle ultrastructural changes in vulnerable CA1 hippocampal synapses, including reduced pre-synapse size and decreased synaptic vesicle density, which suggest that chronic SD modifies synaptic transmission and plasticity. Together, our findings indicate that chronic SD differentially impacts the brain and the synaptic proteome, nominating candidate therapeutic targets and signaling pathways for future mechanistic studies of chronic SD and how SD contributes to increased AD risk.

papers.title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
papers.abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

papers.title: Biological Signaling Pathways Associated with Late Tendon Development in Chicken Embryos and Their Dependence on Mechanical Stimulation
papers.abstract: During embryonic and neonatal development, tendons exhibit rapid changes in mechanics and structure, including increases in collagen content, crosslinking, and fibril length. These functional and structural changes are partly dependent on mechanical stimulation. However, the specific mechanobiological mechanisms driving these changes remain poorly understood. The objective of this study was to identify the potential biological mechanisms and pathways driving tendon maturation into load-bearing materials using an embryonic chick model. Using bulk RNA sequencing, gene set enrichment analysis, and transcription factor analysis, we produced a transcriptomic profile of chick hindlimb tendons during late embryonic development (E16, E18, and E20) and tendons from rigid and flaccid paralysis-treated embryos. Additionally, we assessed the results from two differential expression analysis models to improve the replicability of our findings. Our results suggest that the largest transcriptomic response occurs between embryonic day 16 and 20, and that among paralysis conditions, rigid paralysis produces the greatest effect relative to controls. Across development, we found positive enrichment in processes related to mechanotransduction, extracellular matrix remodeling, cell adhesion, and contractility, and identified candidate pathways upregulated with development, including TGF-{beta}, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, Hippo, circadian rhythm, and focal adhesion signaling. In paralysis-treated embryos, our data suggest impairment in extracellular matrix remodeling and mechanotransduction events. Specifically, we found that both modes of paralysis are associated with a cellular stress response and downregulation of WNT signaling. Together, our findings identify candidate mechanotransduction pathways that are associated with late tendon maturation and altered by paralysis, which may inform tendon tissue engineering and regenerative approaches.

papers.title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

papers.title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
papers.abstract: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

papers.title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Toolbox
papers.abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

papers.title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
papers.abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

papers.title: Intrinsic timekeeping in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks allow organisms to anticipate predictable environmental changes across the day-night cycle. Here we show that the bacterium Escherichia coli exhibits intrinsic timekeeping that anticipates daily temperature cycles. E. coli biofilms entrained to daily temperature shifts, producing 24-hour rhythms in curli plaque formation that persisted under constant temperature. Mechanistically, genetic analyses localized the autonomous timing machinery to the Rcs phosphorelay, which exhibits structural and conceptual parallels with other circadian systems. The BluFR sensory pathway, which acts upstream of the Rcs phosphorelay, linked temperature and blue-light cycles to rhythmic curli production. Flagellar promoter activity and curli production peaked at opposite times of day, suggesting daily coordination of adhesion and motility programs. These findings identify an intrinsic timing system in E. coli that expands our understanding of biological timekeeping.

papers.title: A microstructural analysis of water intake patterns associated with light phase food and water restriction in male and female rats.
papers.abstract: Water intake is influenced by both eating and circadian rhythms, and the available literature is mixed regarding which variable exerts greater control. Previous reports primarily focused on short term manipulations, however, one study using long term light phase food restriction found that water intake patterns primarily retained circadian characteristics in male rats. To further characterize this behavioral effect, water intake and lick microstructure was analyzed in male and female rats with food access restricted to the light phase. In addition, food and water intake and lick microstructure were analyzed when water access was restricted to the light phase. In support of the previous short term, but not long term, food manipulation studies, when food access was restricted to the light phase most water intake shifted to this time frame. This shift was medicated by increased lick burst number, suggesting altered satiety signaling underling this intake pattern. When water access was restricted to the light phase, food intake was equally distributed across the light and dark phases. There was no effect of sex on the patterns of intake during any test condition. These results further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying food and water-associated and circadian intake patterns by suggesting that altered satiety signaling underlies changes in water intake. Furthermore, these results show that the timing of food access has a greater effect on water intake patterns across the light-dark cycle than water access has on food intake patterns.
